reading.body:
Legal AI has moved from experimentation to deployment, but the profession's defining lesson is that unverified citations invite sanctions, so verification is now the industry standard.

The six reference points span guidance, cataloguing, benchmarking, purchasing data, and academic research. The ABA sets ethics guidance, Legaltech Hub maps the tools, Vals AI benchmarks legal reasoning, ILTA records what firms actually buy, and Stanford CodeX studies the underlying informatics. Together they cover what exists, what works, and what gets deployed.

This matters for AI because legal work is high-stakes text reasoning where errors carry professional liability. Independent benchmarks and ethics opinions act as gatekeepers, not raw model capability. The data does not cover compute, power, or infrastructure costs, and it gives no adoption numbers or performance scores, so it cannot support claims about scaling constraints.

summary: Research, review, and drafting assistance are deployed at scale; sanctions for unverified citations made verification the industry lesson.

analysis.body:
The clearest measured number for this sector comes from the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, which reports 43.9% for Professional, scientific, and technical services, the NAICS 54 grouping that includes legal, against 43.3% in the prior period. That figure is the share of firms answering yes to whether the business used AI in the last two weeks, and the survey first asked the question in September 2023. The Census Bureau does not break the number out for legal services alone, so the profession's own adoption sits somewhere inside a broader professional services aggregate rather than being measured directly.

Where the sources show deployment, it clusters around document and knowledge work. Legaltech Hub describes Relativity rebranding RelativityOne to Relativity aiR in September, launching Relativity claiR in August, acquiring document automation company Gavel in June, and releasing an MCP Connector to Claude or Legal in May. It also describes Steno's Transcript Genius, a deposition transcript analysis tool that mines deposition and trial transcripts for summaries, data points, and strategic insights, and MiAI Law, an Australian platform combining case law research, legislative research, case summarization, contract review, and document and pleading verification. ILTA, the International Legal Technology Association, writes that AI has matured rapidly since the early days of LLMs, and notes Epiq's announcement of Model Context Protocol connectors for Epiq AI, Epiq Discover, Epiq Narrate, and Epiq Access.

Vendor attention is concentrating on the largest firms and on connecting models to proprietary material. Legaltech Hub reports that OpenAI's Astra for Law was built initially for Am Law 200 firms and is not a new model but a configuration pairing GPT-6 Astra with knowledge, tools, and ecosystem plugins tailored for legal. NetDocuments is building its AI strategy around a Legal Context Graph launched in May, arguing that as models and legal tools become more interchangeable, the advantage shifts to firms that can connect AI to their own documents, knowledge, and legal authorities. Legaltech Hub itself exists as a global directory where buyers research legal technology, vendors showcase solutions, and investors understand the marketplace, which is a fair description of where the commercial energy sits.

Independent measurement is thin but pointed. Vals AI runs evaluations on real-world tasks and reports cost per test alongside accuracy, and its results show how quickly price separates from capability: GPT-6 Luna places #20 of 65 on the Vals Index at 58.45% and $0.42 per test, roughly 18x cheaper than GPT-6 Sol at 62.57% and $7.56. MiMo V2.6 Flash places #16 of 65 at 59.58% and $0.20 per test, with MiMo V2.6 Pro at #17 at 59.47% and $0.39 per test, the top-scoring open-weight models on the Index. Vals AI also reports that a model it tested was slowest on routine knowledge work such as MedCode, Legal Research and Public Benefits Bench, a reminder that legal research is a latency-sensitive workload. This site's own catalogue tracks the 1000 most-downloaded open legal models on the Hugging Face Hub, refreshed daily from the Hub's public API, which measures developer interest rather than firm deployment.

The profession's guidance comes from the American Bar Association. Its Task Force on Law and Artificial Intelligence focused on six issues, AI and the Profession, AI Risk Management, AI and Access to Justice, AI Governance, AI Challenges with Generative AI, and AI and Legal Education, and has concluded its work. The ABA Center for Innovation says it will continue to address AI's impact on the profession and the practice of law, including related ethical considerations, provide guidance on trustworthy and responsible development and use, and identify strategies to mitigate AI-related risks, and the Center's AI work, including Formal Opinion 512 on generative AI ethics, is described as the profession's reference point. Stanford CodeX, a partnership between the Law School and the Department of Computer Science, frames the same territory academically, with an international conference uniting legal experts, policymakers, and business leaders to harness AI for sustainable, ethical, and responsible legal systems, and FutureLaw 2026.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material supports a few practical moves rather than a verdict. Check the Census Bureau figure for what it is, a NAICS 54 aggregate that includes legal rather than a legal-specific rate. Use Legaltech Hub to see what exists before evaluating what works, and ILTA's annual technology survey as the record of actual purchasing and deployment across law firms. Treat Vals AI's independent evaluations as the vendor-neutral test of whether legal AI actually reasons, on legal research, case-law synthesis, and statutory interpretation, and read cost per test alongside accuracy. Then follow the ABA's guidance on trustworthy and responsible use and on mitigating AI-related risk. The sources here report adoption, tooling, pricing, and ethics guidance; they report little on realized return on investment, so any ROI claim should be treated as unsupported by this material.

https://www.iltanet.org/.brief: ILTA, which calls itself a trusted global resource community for legal technologists, observes that AI has matured rapidly since the early days of LLMs and that its Spring Peer to Peer topics reflect this evolution. Epiq announced the availability of Model Context Protocol connectors for Epiq AI, Epiq Discover, Epiq Narrate, and Epiq Access. Litify says its ACE product now offers firm-wide AI reasoning, workflow automation, multi-step agents, and cross-platform connectivity for legal teams.

https://www.legaltechnologyhub.com/.brief: Legaltech Hub describes itself as a global directory of legal technology solutions, tools and services, serving buyers researching legal tech, vendors showcasing their products, and investors seeking to understand the marketplace. The site reports a high-level comparison of frontier models' AI offerings for the legal industry, based on information available as of September 29, 2026 and drawn chiefly from provider announcements and its own reporting, with an in-depth comparison of four providers reserved for Premium subscribers. It notes that Relativity made a series of AI announcements ahead of RelFest 2026 in Chicago, including rebranding RelativityOne as Relativity aiR in September, launching Relativity claiR in August, acquiring document automation company Gavel in June, and releasing an MCP connector in May. NetDocuments, the site says, is building its AI strategy around a Legal Context Graph launched in May, supported by a new benchmark and two AI features. The site also reports that OpenAI has released Astra for Law, built initially for Am Law 200 firms as a configuration pairing its GPT-6 Astra model with legal-specific knowledge, tools and plugins, and carries an interview with Steno's James Ehlers about the Transcript Genius deposition transcript analysis tool.

https://law.stanford.edu/codex-the-stanf.brief: CodeX is a partnership between Stanford Law School and the Department of Computer Science that studies how information technology can improve legal processes. It applies data science and artificial intelligence to build quantitative and predictive models of the law, moving beyond traditional empirical analysis. The program offers a hands-on accelerated track for interdisciplinary student teams to prototype Agentic AI and the CFAA applications at the intersection of technology and law. CodeX also hosts a hackathon that brings together AI innovators, machine learning specialists, and legal professionals to prototype future legal technology. Additionally, it organizes an international conference and FutureLaw 2026 to bring together leaders in law, technology, and policy to discuss sustainable, ethical, and responsible AI in legal systems.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/te.brief: The World of AI catalogues what it calls the 1000 most-downloaded open legal models on the Hugging Face Hub, listing each one's licence, download count and release date. It says the catalogue is rebuilt daily from the Hub's public API, sorted by all-time downloads, with every model linking to its own Hub page. The page records its last verification date as 2026-09-28. It also advertises books and consulting services, and describes the wider site as an atlas of what the law says, who is suing whom and what the words mean, rebuilt daily from primary sources.

https://www.americanbar.org/groups/cente.brief: The Task Force on Law and Artificial Intelligence has finished its work, and the Center for Innovation will keep addressing how AI affects the legal profession, including ethical issues, trustworthy development, and risk-mitigation strategies. It will also provide guidance on responsible AI use. Past webinars from the Task Force examine how AI is reshaping law practice, covering practical applications, new legal technology, and the ethical, professional-responsibility, and regulatory challenges lawyers must navigate.
